The shift toward remote work that began as an emergency measure has settled into something more permanent, and organizations are still working out what that means for how knowledge moves between people. When everyone sat in the same building, information traveled through overheard conversations, whiteboard sketches left up for a week, and the casual question asked on the way to the coffee machine. None of that was written down, and almost none of it needed to be.

Distributed teams lost those channels overnight. What replaced them was documentation: wikis, recorded meetings, threaded discussions, decision logs. The volume of written material produced by a typical product team has grown several times over in a few years, and the growth shows no sign of slowing. This has quietly created a new problem that few organizations have named, let alone solved.

The problem is not that information is missing. It is that the information exists in forms that resist retrieval. A decision made in a recorded call lives forty minutes into a video nobody will rewatch. The reasoning behind an architecture choice is spread across a dozen chat messages, two documents, and a diagram that only makes sense with the surrounding conversation. When a new person joins the team, they inherit access to everything and understanding of almost nothing.

Search was supposed to fix this, and for a certain class of question it does. If you know the name of the thing you are looking for, full-text search will usually find it. But the questions that matter most are rarely of that kind. They are questions like why did we choose this approach, what did we already try, and who knows about this. Answering them requires assembling context from fragments that no single search query will surface together.

The recent wave of language-model tools promises to close this gap, and in demonstrations it often appears to. Ask a question, get a synthesized answer drawn from your organization's knowledge. The demonstrations, however, share a quiet dependency: they work only as well as the preparation of the material they draw from. Feed the model well-organized, well-bounded pieces of information and the answers are impressive. Feed it arbitrary fragments produced by mechanical splitting and the answers acquire a characteristic vagueness, correct in outline and wrong in the particulars.

That preparation step turns out to be where most of the difficulty lives. Breaking a body of material into pieces sounds like a formality, but every boundary is a small editorial decision about what belongs together. Cut a passage in the wrong place and the claim loses the qualification that followed it, the number loses the unit that preceded it, or the answer loses the question it was answering. Multiply that by a few thousand documents and the cumulative loss is no longer noise; it is the difference between a system people trust and one they quietly stop using.

There is a temptation to treat this as a problem that bigger models will simply absorb, and to some extent longer context windows do soften it. But the economics run the other way. The organizations with the most to gain from these tools are precisely the ones with the most material, and the cost of feeding everything to a model scales with volume while the value of any given fragment does not. Selection, and therefore preparation, remains the binding constraint.

What seems likely is that the preparation of organizational knowledge becomes a discipline of its own, the way data engineering did a decade earlier. The teams that treat it seriously, that preserve the connections between a conclusion and its evidence, between a chart and the discussion of it, will get compounding returns from every tool built on top. The teams that treat it as a checkbox will keep wondering why the impressive demonstration never quite survived contact with their own material.
